case_study_insert.main_stem: Vital Roots Meal Prep (VRM) is a private limited company in the consumer services sector, specialising in plant-based meal-prep delivery, employing a workforce of 52. Founded in 2020 by Sofia Marin, VRM prepares and delivers weekly plant-based meal boxes across the Bristol region and uses a hierarchical structure with autocratic leadership. VRM plans to invest $780,000 in a second kitchen with a refrigerated delivery fleet, financed by a $450,000 hire purchase agreement on the vans and $330,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $247,500 a year, a variable cost of $7.25 a unit and a selling price of $12.75, and currently produces 96,000 units a year (meal boxes). VRM faces two problems: food waste of 7.4% in the kitchen and labour turnover of 19% among delivery drivers.
case_study_insert.appendix_1_marketing_ops: Quality and Waste Report — Q3 2025: The Bristol kitchen packed 24,000 meal boxes last quarter at a mislabel and wrong-item defect rate of 2.2%, down from 3.6% a year ago. Food waste fell from 9.1% to 7.4% but remains above the 5% target. Customer complaints fell from 41 to 23 per month. A market research survey of 650 subscribers found 63% would pay up to $1.50 more per box for fully compostable packaging, and 49% of new customers cite plant-based health benefits. Average delivery time is 1.8 days. On-the-job training in food-safety is incomplete for 16 of 52 staff; off-the-job training courses at the culinary college cost $750 per employee.

appendix_2_financial_data.title: Extract from the Statement of Profit or Loss and Capital employed data of Vital Roots Meal Prep for the year ended 31 March 2025 ($ '000)

case_study_insert.appendix_3_external_environment: Economic and Business Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The central bank has raised the base interest rate from 3.75% to 4.5%, increasing borrowing costs for businesses with variable-rate loans and hire purchase. (2) The national minimum wage will rise by 6.4% from $12.50 to $13.30 per hour from April 2026, raising wage bills across food delivery and kitchens. (3) Plant-protein and compostable packaging input costs have risen 11.2% year-on-year, food inflation is running at 7.8%, and consumer spending on plant-based products grew 6.1% in the same period.

questions.question_text: VRM plans to finance part of its second kitchen with a $450,000 hire purchase agreement on the vans. Explain two advantages for VRM of using retained profit to fund part of the expansion instead of relying on hire purchase.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Using $330,000 of retained profit instead of extending hire purchase costs VRM nothing in interest or finance charges, protecting the $5.50 contribution per meal box at a time when input costs have risen 11.2% and fixed costs already stand at $247,500 a year. Every dollar not paid as hire-purchase interest can absorb the plant-protein and compostable-packaging inflation or fund the new kitchen's launch marketing, helping VRM keep its $12.75 price competitive against other meal-prep firms.

Point 2: Retained profit carries no repossession risk on the refrigerated vans if weekly payments are missed or demand dips over winter, so VRM keeps full ownership and control of the delivery fleet from day one. It also avoids adding to the hire-purchase burden at a time when the base interest rate has risen from 3.75% to 4.5% — interest payable already rose from $15,000 to $24,000 — and unlike external finance it imposes no usage mileage or maintenance conditions on how the second kitchen and its vans are operated.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation and analysis applied to Vital Roots Meal Prep and its expansion decision.

questions.question_text: VRM is launching its second kitchen and expanded delivery zone. Consider a national television campaign, local radio sponsorship, or social media influencer marketing. Which should VRM choose to promote the launch? Justify your recommendation.
questions.model_answer:
Television campaign: A national television campaign would put the Vital Roots brand in front of millions of viewers quickly and could build strong awareness of the plant-based subscription offer. However, VRM is a 52-employee regional business funding a $780,000 expansion; national production and airtime costs are extremely high, and most viewers live far outside the Bristol delivery zone, where delivery time averages 1.8 days — distant customers cannot receive fresh boxes, so spend would be largely wasted. Television also suits mass FMCG brands, not subscription meal services that need targeted sign-ups.

Local radio sponsorship: Local radio is far cheaper, reaches Bristol-area commuters repeatedly at breakfast and drive-time, and suits messages such as subscription discounts for new postcodes. Its limitation is narrow and aging reach; the health-conscious plant-based audience skews younger, and local radio cannot build the national brand reputation VRM needs for wholesale or multi-site growth, nor target by diet or delivery postcode.

Social media influencer marketing: Working with Bristol-based nutritionists, chefs and fitness creators targets exactly the 63% of surveyed subscribers interested in fully compostable packaging and the 49% who cite plant-based health benefits, with measurable sign-ups and strong storytelling potential around defect-rate improvements (3.6% to 2.2%) and food waste falling from 9.1% to 7.4%. Results are slower to compound than TV and depend on influencer credibility, but cost per acquired subscriber is low and conversion can be tracked directly through discount codes.

Recommendation: VRM should choose social media influencer marketing. It reaches the precise segment identified in its research (63% packaging interest, 49% health motivation), costs far less than television for a 52-employee regional operator, scales across all new postcodes faster than local radio, and lets VRM show the second kitchen's quality improvements. Television is rejected as unaffordable and untargeted beyond the delivery zone; local radio is rejected as the lead channel because its audience skews older and cannot be geo-targeted to new routes, though short drive-time bursts could support the launch. Influencers alone lack broadcast reach, so VRM should pair them with introductory subscriber offers and referral discounts.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Limited knowledge or outline of the promotional options with minimal context.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Detailed discussion of the advantages and disadvantages of at least two options in the context of VRM with some judgement.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed discussion of all three options in the context of VRM with a well-justified recommendation explaining why television and radio are rejected.

questions.question_text: VRM's labour turnover is 19% among delivery drivers and food waste of 7.4% persists in the kitchen. Explain two benefits for VRM of autocratic leadership in this context.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Autocratic leadership gives VRM fast, clear decisions on route planning, load-out and fridge temperature protocols — essential when drivers leave the kitchen on tight 1.8-day delivery windows and when food-safety (food-safety) breaches could destroy the whole brand. A single decisive manager can re-plan deliveries mid-week without committee delay, directly protecting delivery reliability and the fall in complaints from 41 to 23 per month.

Point 2: Autocratic direction keeps kitchen routines disciplined and uniform, which is exactly what VRM needs to push food waste below the 7.4% level and toward the 5% target: one standard for portioning, stock rotation and labelling, enforced consistently across pickers and packers. In a 52-person operation with 16 of 52 staff still untrained in food-safety, clear instruction reduces errors quickly, contains the 2.2% mislabel defect rate and tightens portion control, while turnover of 19% is addressed through induction and pay review rather than diluted decision-making.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid benefit identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to VRM's waste, turnover, defects and delivery targets.

questions.question_text: VRM must train 16 kitchen staff on food-safety procedures. Consider on-the-job training or off-the-job training at the culinary college. Which should VRM choose? Justify your decision.
questions.model_answer:
On-the-job training: Training in the kitchen itself is directly relevant to VRM's own recipes, labelling and fridge-temperature routines, costs nothing in course fees, and keeps the 16 staff productive, protecting output of 24,000 meal boxes last quarter and the 1.8-day delivery promise. Drawbacks are that senior kitchen staff lose preparation time while training others, bad habits can spread between pickers, and no external certificate is awarded — a problem if a retail partner audits food-safety compliance or if VRM wants to prove standards to insurers after any contamination incident.

Off-the-job training: The culinary college course at $750 per employee gives structured, current food-safety certification for all 16 staff, costing $12,000 in total — affordable against a $780,000 second-kitchen investment. It removes kitchen staff from production, however, reducing short-term capacity during peak subscription weeks, and the generic content may not match VRM's exact labelling and allergen workflows, so follow-up on-site coaching would still be needed.

Decision: VRM should choose on-the-job training for the bulk of the 16 staff, supported by off-the-job culinary college places for two supervisors who can then deliver refresher food-safety sessions in-house. On-the-job training is cheapest, kitchen-specific and avoids cutting into delivery capacity while turnover is 19% and waste is above target. Full off-the-job training is rejected because withdrawing 16 staff and spending $12,000 up front would strain the launch of the second kitchen; college certification can be phased in once the 2.2% defect rate and 7.4% waste figure move decisively downward and the second kitchen reaches stable output.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Basic description of the two training methods with limited application to VRM.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Detailed analysis of the benefits and drawbacks of one or both training methods in the context of VRM.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Comprehensive evaluation of both training methods in the context of VRM with a well-justified decision covering cost, capacity, certification and compliance.

questions.question_text: Calculate and explain how VRM's management can use its cost, break-even and productivity data.

sub_parts.model_answer: Formula: Break-even output = Fixed costs ÷ Contribution per unit. Substitution: $247,500 ÷ ($12.75 − $7.25) = $247,500 ÷ $5.50 = 45,000 units. Answer: break-even output is 45,000 units a year.
Formula: Contribution per unit = Selling price − Variable cost per unit. Substitution: $12.75 − $7.25 = $5.50. Answer: contribution per unit is $5.50.

sub_parts.question_text: Explain four ways VRM's management can use this financial data.
sub_parts.model_answer:
1. VRM's managers can compare the 45,000-unit break-even output with actual output of 96,000 meal boxes to confirm the business is comfortably profitable, with a margin of safety of 51,000 units, informing how quickly the second kitchen can be opened and staffed without stretching cash.
2. Contribution per unit of $5.50 lets managers model the effect of a fully compostable packaging upsell, for example adding the $1.50 premium would lift contribution to $7.00, letting managers test whether the 63% of subscribers willing to pay more would cover the extra packaging cost and still clear the $247,500 fixed costs.
3. Knowing fixed costs and contribution per unit helps managers set subscription-volume targets used to justify the $450,000 hire purchase agreement on the vans and the $330,000 retained-profit contribution, checking the new kitchen can service both before the launch is announced.
4. Managers can use unit cost data ($247,500 ÷ 96,000 units + $7.25 = $9.83 a unit) to benchmark performance across quarters, identify where food waste above the 7.4% level is pushing costs up, and renegotiate plant-protein supply contracts amid the 11.2% input-cost inflation.

questions.model_answer: (i) Break-even output = 45,000 units | (ii) Contribution per unit = $5.50 | (iii) Four contextual uses explained: margin of safety of 51,000 units vs 96,000-unit output; compostable-packaging premium modelling vs $247,500 fixed costs; hire-purchase feasibility for the $780,000 expansion; and unit-cost benchmarking at $9.83 to tackle waste and input inflation.

working_marks: 1 mark for correct formula/method, 1 mark for accurate numerical answer in (i) and (ii). 1 mark per valid applied point in (iii).

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 2, evaluate VRM's financial performance by calculating the gross profit margin, the profit margin and ROCE for 2024 and 2025. Has VRM's financial performance improved? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Calculations:
Gross Profit Margin 2024 = 30.0%
Gross Profit Margin 2025 = 37.5%
Profit Margin 2024 = 10.0%
Profit Margin 2025 = 12.5%
ROCE 2024 = 8.0%
ROCE 2025 = 10.0%

Detailed workings: 2024 gross profit $324,000 on revenue $1,080,000 (cost of sales $756,000); 2025 gross profit $459,000 on revenue $1,224,000 (cost of sales $765,000). 2024 operating profit $108,000; 2025 operating profit $153,000. 2024 capital employed $1,350,000; 2025 capital employed $1,530,000. Interest payable rose from $15,000 to $24,000, reflecting the hire purchase agreement on the refrigerated vans.

Evaluation: Performance improved, though from a low base. Gross profit grew $135,000 (41.7%) as revenue rose $144,000 and the cost of sales share of revenue fell from 70.0% to 62.5%, helped by the defect rate falling from 3.6% to 2.2%, food waste dropping from 9.1% to 7.4% and complaints from 41 to 23 a month. Operating profit grew 41.7% ($108,000 to $153,000), roughly in line with gross profit growth, so overheads were broadly stable per box. Capital employed rose $180,000 on the second kitchen and van fleet, and the return on that capital improved from 8.0% to 10.0%. However, a capital return of 10.0% is still modest, margins remain thin for a food business, interest payable is rising with the hire purchase and the base-rate move from 3.75% to 4.5%, and the 11.2% plant-protein inflation could squeeze the 37.5% gross margin if VRM cannot pass costs through.

Conclusion: Yes, VRM's financial performance has improved — revenue, gross profit and operating profit all grew, cost of sales was genuinely controlled, and the return on capital employed rose from 8.0% to 10.0%. The improvement is not yet comfortable: margins are thin and input inflation is running well ahead of price rises, so VRM should push the compostable-packaging premium ($1.50), cut waste below the 5% target, and watch van finance costs closely, or the gains seen in 2025 will unwind.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: States financial figures or changes without accurate ratio calculations.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Accurately calculates the gross profit margin, profit margin and ROCE for both 2024 and 2025 with contextual analysis of the trend.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Accurate ratio calculations for both years combined with detailed evaluation of revenue, cost of sales, overheads and capital employed movements and a justified conclusion on whether VRM's financial performance improved.

questions.question_text: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for VRM of introducing fully compostable packaging for its meal boxes.
questions.model_answer:
Advantage: Fully compostable packaging matches the preference of the 63% of surveyed subscribers who would pay up to $1.50 more per box, allowing VRM to add the premium, protect its $5.50 contribution per box even as input costs rise 11.2%, and differentiate from competitors still using plastic. It also strengthens VRM's brand with the 49% of new customers motivated by plant-based health and sustainability, deepening loyalty and lowering the 19% driver turnover's knock-on effect on service reliability — customers tolerate minor delays from a brand they believe in.

Disadvantage: Compostable materials cost more than conventional plastic, increasing the $7.25 variable cost per box and squeezing margins unless the $1.50 premium is accepted by enough subscribers or backed by the new second-kitchen scale. Any failure in the new packaging — weaker seals, shorter chill life or leaks in transit — would also raise the 2.2% mislabel/defect rate, increase food waste above the 7.4% level and destroy the 1.8-day delivery promise that underpins VRM's reputation with retail and corporate customers.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for a valid advantage and 1 mark for a valid disadvantage.
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to VRM's research data, costs and expansion.

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the interest rate rise to 4.5%, the 6.4% minimum wage increase and the 11.2% rise in input costs will affect VRM. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Interest rate rise (3.75% to 4.5%): If the $450,000 hire purchase agreement on the vans is variable-rate, the 0.75 percentage point rise adds about $3,400 a year to finance costs — real but modest next to $247,500 of fixed costs. Higher rates also make further borrowing for a third kitchen more expensive, could raise the cost of renewing the fleet, and may temper consumer appetite for subscription meal services, slowing the 6.1% growth in plant-based spending. VRM can fix the hire-purchase rate or accelerate retained-profit repayments to limit exposure.

Minimum wage increase (6.4%, to $13.30 per hour): VRM employs 52 staff, many drivers, pickers and kitchen operatives near or below middle-band wages. If roughly 30 of the 52 staff sit close to the minimum wage on 40-hour weeks, the 6.4% rise adds roughly $1,660 per affected worker a year — around $50,000 a year — on top of 19% driver turnover already inflating recruitment and onboarding costs. This is materially larger than the rate impact and lands directly on VRM's largest cost line, wages, though many Bristol drivers are paid above minimum.

Input cost inflation (11.2% plant-protein and compostable packaging): VRM's variable cost of $7.25 a unit is dominated by plant proteins, grains, fresh produce and packaging. An 11.2% rise on, say, 70% of the variable cost ($5.08) adds roughly $0.57 per box; at 96,000 boxes a year that is about $55,000 a year, cutting contribution per unit from $5.50 toward $4.93 and eroding roughly 10% of margin. With 6.1% growth in plant-based spending intact, VRM can pass through part of the increase via the $1.50 compostable premium, but full pass-through would surrender its price edge against own-label supermarket ready meals.

Conclusion: The 11.2% rise in input costs will have the greatest impact. It strikes every one of the 96,000 boxes, totalling roughly $55,000 a year and steadily eroding the $5.50 contribution margin that justifies the $780,000 second-kitchen expansion. The minimum wage rise is the second most serious risk, around $50,000 a year on support and delivery roles and amplified by 19% turnover, while the interest-rate increase is the smallest in cash terms (roughly $3,400 a year) and can be managed by fixing the hire-purchase rate. VRM should therefore renegotiate protein supply contracts, push the compostable premium and optimise routes — or the gross-margin gains in Appendix 2 will be reversed within a year.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Identifies the external factors with limited application to VRM.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the impact of at least two external changes on VRM's costs, revenue or financing in context.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three external changes in the context of VRM with a well-justified judgement that input-cost inflation has the greatest impact and why the other two are smaller.
